rows.description: A young adult presses fingers spread on a table to steady nerves or uses a fidget object to stay calm, a healthy regulation tool that observers should not mistake for disinterest.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult reads the thumbs-up, folded-hands and wave emoji as modern equivalents of gestures, but the thumbs-up may seem curt or passive-aggressive to some. Norms differ by age and workplace.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult travelling finds that the OK-sign, thumbs-up and beckoning finger carry different meanings in different countries, some offensive. When unsure, a smile, a word or a namaste-like neutral greeting is safer.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A student abroad learns that an upturned-finger beckon that is friendly in one place can be rude in another, and a palm-down scoop is common in South Asia and elsewhere. Guessing meaning from one culture is risky, so watching locals and asking is wiser.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
rows.description: A young adult in a seminar lifts a finger, leans in slightly or catches the chair's eye to claim a turn. Read together, these cues show wish to contribute; interrupting anyway shows poor turn reading, while patient signalling builds influence.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult in a presentation uses measured hand shapes to show a graph trend or process, but fidgety or over-large motions can distract. Purposeful gestures usually help listeners follow, and rehearsing on video can show what to trim.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A student meeting a Deaf friend learns that signed languages use shape, movement, space and facial grammar as complete languages, not mime. Treating signs as loose gestures shows misunderstanding; learning basics and asking respectfully builds connection.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A student reads a friend leaning forward as interest and leaning back as relaxed or distant. These are weak cues; a person leaning back may be comfortable, or unwell, so checking with a question is wiser than concluding disinterest.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult stiffens, holds the breath or hunches in a stressful exam or confrontation. It signals threat or anxiety; slow exhaling, dropping the shoulders and grounding the feet often ease it.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26
related mind states: anxiety, relief from stress

rows.subtype: Bowing, folding hands and formal movement [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young adult uses a bow, namaste or a stand-up greeting according to custom. Meaning is politeness and respect, but the depth and manner vary by place and relationship, so watching others and following local custom avoids offence.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26
